title: Confession and the Stillness of Castlemaine
summary: Carla dal Forno discusses her fourth solo album, moving from the city to Castlemaine, recording in a disused hospital and the relationship between sound, place and stillness.
transcript:
Carla dal Forno joined Lauren and Simon in the Triple R studios on 23 April 2026 — the day before her fourth solo album, Confession, arrived on her own Kallista Records, and between two launch shows at Hope St Radio. This transcript has been edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Welcome to the Triple R studios.

Carla: Thanks Lauren, it's great to be here.

Lauren: We should mention we just played 'Going Out', from the brand new record, too.

Simon: We're thrilled and honoured to have you here. By way of introduction, for those coming to your music more recently: you're an extraordinary musician and visual artist. You grew up in Melbourne, spent a number of years overseas in Berlin and London, and more recently you've been living in Castlemaine, in central Victoria — with four solo albums to date, including Confession, out tomorrow on your own label, Kallista Records. We're excited to talk about the process and the themes and the ideas. But first — you're in town for these launch shows, and tonight is only your third Melbourne show since you got back, isn't it?

Carla: Yeah — in almost a decade. I was away for a while, and didn't play any shows in Melbourne for a long time. It's been great to come back and play in the city that made me a musician in the first place.

Simon: And at Hope St Radio last night, there was a pasta dish created in your honour. How did the show go?

Carla: The pasta was delicious. And the show was great — I'd never been to that space before, and it really feels like someone's lounge room. It's so intimate. It just felt like playing for my friends.

Lauren: You're back at Hope St again tonight. Pasta on the menu again, or are they going to shake it up?

Carla: I think it's pasta again. I'm not sure what type — I'm excited to see.

Lauren: We saw the special mix you did last weekend for Crack Magazine's Sunday Mix — a really beautiful selection of what you called Aussie pop bangers, with great stuff from Chateau, The Lewers, The Stroppies, and Who Cares?, who we've got lined up to play shortly. You said you'd enjoyed the humour in these songs, and that Sunday felt like a good day to have a laugh while listening to music. Can you tell us more about the selection?

Carla: I really wanted to put some of my favourite Australian artists on that mix. It's a UK publication, so I thought some of its readers might not have heard these artists — artists I just think are brilliant, and who should be more widely known.

Lauren: Is humour important to you in your own music?

Carla: It definitely is. It's maybe not the most overt quality of my music, but when I'm writing lyrics I'm often giggling at what I'm writing. If something feels humorous and funny, I enjoy that.

Lauren: You also featured on Moopie's A Colourful Storm compilation Going Back to Sleep — your track 'Veselka City Lights' sat alongside a lot of that same community of artists. That scene feels like it's become a real creative home for you since you've been back in Australia. Can you tell us about the connection?

Carla: I've known Moopie for maybe ten years now, and maintained contact with him because he's a touring DJ — I'd see him in London and Berlin. He's done such a great job with that label: so many interesting artists, from varied genres and backgrounds, but they all tie together. And I was so happy to be part of that release in particular. Everyone's obsessed with Who Cares? at the moment — I am similarly — and The Lewers as well. When I heard those names were going to be on it, I definitely wanted to be part of it.

Simon: You and Moopie seem very philosophically aligned about shining a light on these artists — which you also do through your own radio broadcasting. But I'm keen to talk about Confession. The press material describes it as being about a friendship that became emotionally charged in an unexpected way, and you've said you originally set out to make something more veiled, but found the songs really worked when you leaned into a more direct emotional truth.

Carla: That's true. I had a break from songwriting for a while because I had a baby, and when I got back into the studio, talking about my personal life felt like too much hard work. I wanted it to be a bit more removed — I didn't want to have to be too vulnerable in my songwriting. But when the songs started to work, it felt like I was practising having conversations that I wanted to have with people in real life. That's been a theme in my past work as well, even going back to my first album, but it felt much more present here. That felt like the narrative arc of this record.

Lauren: And you recorded in a partially decommissioned 1930s hospital in Castlemaine, is that right?

Carla: Yeah — there's an old hospital there that's been turned into a workspace, so there are lots of different artists and musicians, and many different acupuncturists and massage therapists, and we all have little studio spaces squirreled away in this building. It hasn't had any development in what feels like fifty years — it's really quite dilapidated in parts — but it's wonderful. I'd never had a studio off-site before, and I really appreciated that. A room of one's own, they say. It's a classic, but it's true.

Simon: You're such a creative person across disciplines — you studied fine arts before focusing on music — and we understand some of these songs were written during afternoons spent painting.

Carla: Yeah, there was one song in particular where I was just having a really great time on my own, painting. That song, 'I Go Back', I wrote at the end of the album, when I was coming to this place of really enjoying my own company, and I wanted to say something about that. I remember last time I was on this show you asked me why I write songs about being in nature, and I just blanked — I froze. I thought, that's such a great question, and I have no answer for it. But it's a theme I keep returning to. The relationship with nature can be so multifaceted: it can be a place of nurture and self-awareness, and also danger and excitement.

Lauren: When you were making your last album, Come Around, you talked about seeing Clarice Beckett's paintings at the Castlemaine Art Museum, and wanting to transport that hazy atmosphere into your own work. Are there visual references you'd identify as important to the new record?

Carla: Oh, that's a great question... and I'm drawing a blank again. You've done it to me again! No — Clarice Beckett is still such a touchstone. I go to the Castlemaine Art Museum all the time, just to look at the paintings they have there; we're really lucky they have a few in the permanent collection. And something about her being a Victorian artist — I really relate to that. Her work is about mood and atmosphere and stillness, and I connect with that. It's a similar ambition for me, in what I want to create sonically.

Simon: Highly recommended, if people aren't familiar with her work — such an evocative catalogue. Another moment on the record that's really stayed with us is 'Under the Covers', the beautiful second single, which has just come out. You've described it as almost a voice memo for your partner — an ode to steady, long-term love that celebrates both the mundane and the exciting moments of a relationship, which you've said isn't often explored in music. Can you tell us about the song and its place on the album?

Carla: I really loved writing this song. The other songs on the album feel a little more edgy — I'm unpacking feelings that are a bit more uncomfortable — and this one felt really breezy and fun to write, because I was telling my partner what I appreciate about this life we've created together, and the intimacy that you have when you've known someone for a long time.

Lauren: Beautiful.

Simon: There's a Sunnyboys cover on the record as well. What's the personal significance of 'Alone With You'?

Carla: My dad was in a band in the eighties, and his band supported the Sunnyboys a number of times when they played in Melbourne. So there was this family mythology around the band, and I've grown up listening to them. That song in particular has always been a favourite, and I feel like it was just waiting for me to cover it. I really felt like I had to do it at some point.

Simon: Tonight's show is at Hope St Radio in Collingwood again, with Blue Communications — who we heard from just before — and Early World. Can you tell us about your relationships with those two bands?

Carla: Early World had their first performance ever last night. It's Mary MacDougall and Francis Plagne — Mary's in Warm Currency, which is one of my favourite bands, and Francis is this prolific, amazing artist with many varied projects. They played a great show, and it was such a treat to see what they're creating together. I hope everyone gets to hear it soon. And Blue Communications — I know Billie from Spice World, who sent me the album last year, and I thought: this is incredible for a first album from a new band. That Australian summer song — if it had been released in the eighties, I reckon it would have charted. They're so good. Everyone should come down early for those two.

Simon: And save some room for pasta. You're at the Bridge Hotel in Castlemaine tomorrow night as well. A very big thank you to our guest, Carla dal Forno, for dropping by Triple R for a chat — and congratulations again on the new record. It's really, really beautiful. We're going to hear another track from it now, the one we were just talking about: 'Under the Covers'. Thanks, Carla.

Carla: Thanks.
